summary: Lists requirements for the Path Computation Element Communication Protocol for inter-area MPLS and GMPLS traffic engineering. In multi-area networks, a head-end router cannot compute a constrained path across areas, so a path computation element can help. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: One router only sees its own neighborhood and cannot plan a trip across town. This note says what a helper must do to plan it.

questions: what does pce need for inter-area te
how does pce compute paths across areas
subtitle: How path computation elements help route traffic across multiple network areas

tldr.problem: In large multi-area networks, routers see only their own area's topology and cannot compute paths to distant areas. This breaks traffic engineering, which requires optimal constrained paths across the whole network.
tldr.mechanism: A Path Computation Element (PCE) with visibility across all areas—or multiple PCEs cooperating across areas—can compute optimal inter-area paths and tell the head-end router which path to use.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines detailed requirements for the PCE Communication Protocol to support inter-area path computation, enabling carriers to efficiently route traffic through large hierarchical networks.

today: RFC 4927 is an informational RFC that has not been obsoleted. It defined the scope for PCECP requirements specific to inter-area MPLS and GMPLS traffic engineering. These requirements were incorporated into PCECP standards like RFC 5440. PCE-based inter-area path computation remains in use by carriers and large enterprises operating multi-area networks where traffic engineering is critical.

sections.title: Routing at Scale: The Area Hierarchy
sections.content:
Large networks divide themselves into areas (called OSPF areas or IS-IS levels) to improve scalability. Each area floods its topology only to routers within that area, not to the entire network. This containment of information reduces routing protocol overhead and network size.

The trade-off is clear: a router in one area knows the full topology of its area and reachability information to other areas, but not the detailed topology of those other areas. When a router needs to set up a Traffic Engineered Label Switched Path (TE-LSP)—a path that follows specific constraints like bandwidth and hop count—to a destination in another area, it cannot compute the optimal path because it lacks visibility of that area's internals.

The classic solution, per-domain path computation, uses loose hops and asks Area Border Routers (ABRs) to expand the path as the LSP traverses each area. This works but is inefficient: it may not find the optimal path and can require multiple setup attempts with backtracking.
sections.plainLanguage: Big networks are divided into neighborhoods so routers do not have to know everything. But when a router needs to plan a route across neighborhoods, it hits a wall: it only knows its own area and cannot see inside the others.

sections.title: Key Concepts: PCE and the Communication Protocol
sections.content:
A Path Computation Element (PCE) is a network component that can compute paths given a network topology and constraints. A Path Computation Client (PCC)—typically a head-end router—asks the PCE for paths. The PCE Communication Protocol (PCECP) is the protocol they use to exchange requests and responses.

Two approaches exist. A single-PCE model places a PCE that sees all areas and computes end-to-end paths. A multiple-PCE model distributes PCEs across areas; each PCE sees its area and one PCC might query multiple PCEs, which collaborate to compute an end-to-end path. The multiple-PCE approach is more scalable but demands that PCECP can track which PCEs were involved, record areas crossed, and detect routing loops.
sections.plainLanguage: A PCE is a smart helper that knows the map and can plan routes. Routers ask it for paths. PCEs can work alone (if one knows the whole city) or together (if each knows a few neighborhoods and they talk to each other).

sections.title: Why PCE Solves the Multi-Area Problem
sections.content:
The per-domain approach has two major limitations. First, it does not guarantee the optimal path: because routers expand loose hops based only on local information, the result may not be the shortest constrained path across all areas. Second, it causes setup delays and possible crankback: if an expanded path fails a constraint, the request backs up to the previous ABR, which tries an alternative, leading to multiple setup attempts.

PCE-based computation overcomes these limitations. A PCE with inter-area visibility can compute the true optimal path in one pass. If multiple PCEs cooperate, they do so with awareness of each other's area constraints, so their combined result is still optimal. The PCC gets a response with the best path and can set up the LSP with minimal retries.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way: routers guess at each neighborhood boundary, often guessing wrong. The PCE way: one or a few smart helpers see far enough ahead to pick the best path the first time.

sections.title: Core PCECP Requirements for Inter-Area Paths
sections.content:
The RFC lists nine specific requirements for PCECP. The protocol must allow the PCC to indicate whether area crossing is permitted or required, and it must report back whether the computed path crosses areas. It must identify which areas the path transits and segment the path so each segment is marked with its area. It must distinguish between strict explicit paths (every hop specified) and loose paths (some hops unspecified).

For multiple-PCE scenarios, the protocol must let a PCC specify a preferred list of PCEs per area and must record which PCEs actually computed parts of the path. It must allow the PCC to specify the source and destination areas, include or exclude specific areas from the path, and request diverse paths (link-disjoint, node-disjoint, or SRLG-disjoint) both end-to-end and per-area. Finally, it must include a loop-detection mechanism to prevent request loops when multiple PCEs forward requests to each other.
sections.plainLanguage: PCECP must tell the PCE what kind of path is wanted (crossing areas or not, diverse or not, through certain areas or avoiding them), and the PCE must tell the PCC which areas the path uses and which PCEs helped compute it.

sections.title: Policy Enforcement and Manageability
sections.content:
The RFC requires that request messages include the originating PCC address, so that policies can be applied not just to the peer connection but to the actual originator. This is important in a multiple-PCE scenario where a request might be forwarded through several PCEs.

For management, PCECP MIB modules must track the proportion and success rate of inter-area requests, and in multiple-PCE scenarios, must record the performance of the PCE chain—minimum, maximum, and average response times, and the availability of each PCE. This enables operators to detect which PCE in a chain is causing delays and to troubleshoot failures.
sections.plainLanguage: Network operators need to see which paths are being requested, whether requests succeed, and which helper (PCE) is slow so they can upgrade it.

sections.title: Security and Trust
sections.content:
The RFC notes that IGP areas are typically administrated by the same entity, so the inter-area application does not introduce new security models compared to the generic PCE requirements. However, PCECP must prevent request loops, which could otherwise be exploited to consume resources. It must also ensure that computed paths are loop-free.

The protocol must support mutual authentication between PCCs and PCEs, and between PCEs in a multiple-PCE scenario, to prevent spoofing. Like generic PCECP, it must allow optional security extensions such as IPsec or TLS encryption of control messages.
sections.plainLanguage: PCEs must not trust requests that come in circles, and they must authenticate each other so a rogue PCE cannot redirect traffic.
